The table shown is an excerpt from the DYNR Manual (Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146) and forms the core of the “Input Description” chapter. It systematically lists, in order, each of the input records and sections that a user must employ to control DYNR’s graphical plotting and response-spectrum computations. Below is a field-by-field breakdown, intended to serve as metadata for a RAG-enabled vector store or as a blueprint for automated parsing:

1. Input Description (Section 2)  
   • Acts as the umbrella heading for all records governing data entry.  
   • Spans from section 2.1 through section 2.10 in the manual.  

2. 2.1 Input Language  
   • Defines the overall syntax and conventions of the DYNR input deck.  
   • Likely includes information on record delimiters, line continuation rules, comment syntax, and data‐type conventions (integers, reals, character strings).  

3. 2.2 Input Records  
   • Provides a summary table or list of all valid record names (e.g., SIZE, SCHH, RESP, etc.).  
   • May specify record hierarchy, mandatory vs. optional records, and default behaviors if records are omitted.  

4. 2.3 SIZE – Size and Scale of the Representation  
   • Specifies plot dimensions, scaling factors (linear or logarithmic), axis limits and units.  
   • Typical parameters: X_MIN, X_MAX, Y_MIN, Y_MAX, SCALE_FACTOR, possibly PLOT_UNITS.  

5. 2.4 SCHH – Text Size  
   • Governs annotation styles: font height, style (bold/italic), label orientation, grid text vs. axis text.  
   • Parameters may include TXT_HEIGHT, TXT_FONT, TXT_ANGLE.  

6. 2.5 RESP – Properties of the Single Mass Oscillator  
   • Core settings for response‐spectrum calculation: damping ratio(s), oscillator mass (often set to unity), number of frequency steps.  
   • Keys: DAMPING, FREQUENCY_RANGE, NUM_POINTS, MASS, STIFFNESS.  

7. 2.6 FUNC – External Function  
   • Enables definition of arbitrary excitation time‐histories not already stored in the database.  
   • Likely allows piecewise linear or polynomial specifications, function names, scaling factors.  

8. 2.7 EXCI – Excitation Function  
   • Links stored HIST data or user-defined FUNC to particular loading cases.  
   • Fields: LOAD_ID, DIRECTION (X/Y/Z), SCALE, TIME_OFFSET.  

9. 2.8 SPEC – Response Spectra  
   • Triggers the actual computation and plotting of spectra.  
   • Options for multiple damping values, coordinate directions, and superposition rules.  
   • Parameters: SPEC_ID, DAMPING_SET, FREQ_INCREMENT, OUTPUT_OPTION.  

10. 2.9 HIST – Histogram Curves  
    • Requests extraction and plotting of time‐history curves previously recorded during a DYNA or HYDRA run.  
    • Fields: HIST_ID, ENTITY_TYPE (node, element), DOF or internal force code, load case number.  

11. 2.10 ECHO – Control of the Output Extent  
    • Fine-tunes the verbosity and amount of textual output sent to the listing file.  
    • Options: ECHO_ON/OFF, LEVEL (minimal, normal, detailed), SELECTIVE_ECHO (for specific records).  

By structuring your RAG knowledge base with one document or embedding per record—and including key parameters, default values, permissible ranges, and cross-references—you ensure rapid, context-aware retrieval. Each record can be tagged with its section number, name, description, mandatory/optional status, and typical use cases (e.g., plotting a ground-motion curve vs. computing a 5 %-damped response spectrum). This systematic mapping enables downstream applications—chatbots, automated scripts or validation tools—to guide users in constructing correct DYNR input decks or answering questions about record syntax and interdependencies.

 1 Task Description
 The program DYNR enables the graphical presentation of transient results from the programs DYNA and HYDRA. It plots time-controlled or frequency-controlled results and, as an additional option, calculates response spectra for a given loading or acceleration history.
 Using the input record HIST during a dynamic analysis with the program DYNA one can store in the database the time variations of selected degrees of freedom or internal forces and mo- ments. By the same record HIST, the program HYDRA stores in the database the unsteady temperature or potential variation. DYNR can present these curves graphically in any combi- nation.

Using the input record HIST during a dynamic analysis with the program DYNA one can store in the database the time variations of selected degrees of freedom or internal forces and mo- ments. By the same record HIST, the program HYDRA stores in the database the unsteady temperature or potential variation. DYNR can present these curves graphically in any combi- nation..
 Furthermore, it is capable of using either the already stored acceleration variations of individual points or any newly defined function in order to determine the response spectra.
 A response spectrum is determined by the maximum response of a single mass oscillator with known damping to a known excitation function in relation to the natural frequency of the oscillator.
 Each loading (e.g. earthquake, impact at corner A, impact at corner B, etc.) is stored in DYNA by a certain number.
 DYNR can now plot either the given HIST curves or the response spectra in the various coor- dinate directions under consideration of the various damping values.
Input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics).

The table is a concise “record-item” overview for a family of SOFiSTiK structural‐analysis input records.  Each row names one record (first column) and then lists—left to right—the fixed fields or “items” that must follow when you invoke that record in an input file.  In a Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG) context you would index one document per record, tagging all of its items as searchable metadata.  Below is a breakdown of every record shown:

1.  SIZE  
    •  Items:  
       – DINA   (input geometry unit or scaling factor)  
       – S, W, H   (three “size” parameters, e.g. span, width, height)  
       – MARG   (margin or offset)  
       – FORM   (form or shape code)  
       – TMAX   (maximum thickness or temperature)  

2.  SCHH  
    •  Items H1…H5 in sequence:  
       – H1, H2, H3, H4, H5   (five free‐format header fields)  

3.  RESP  
    •  A more complex record for defining “responses” or results to be printed:  
       – TYPE   (response type code)  
       – D1…D5   (five real “D-group” parameters, e.g. displacements, forces)  
       – C1…C5   (five real “C-group” parameters, e.g. coefficients)  
       – REF1, REF2, REF3   (up to three reference entity numbers)  
       – RC1, RC2, RC3   (three reference component codes)  
       – TMIN, TMAX   (lower and upper thresholds for the response)  
       – TDIF   (tolerance difference or delta)  

4.  FUNC  
    •  Items:  
       – T   (type or flag)  
       – F   (function code)  
       – DT   (data type or date)  
       – NO   (record number)  
       – TITL   (title or comment string)  

5.  EXCI  
    •  Items:  
       – LCS   (local coordinate system ID)  
       – NO   (load or excitation number)  
       – COMP   (component index)  
       – F   (force or amplitude)  
       – TITL   (title or descriptive text)  

6.  SPEC  
    •  Items:  
       – TYPE   (specification type code)  

7.  HIST  
    •  A “history” or time‐series record.  Fields come in fixed columns and define up to ten (0…9) value/case pairs, plus global limits:  
       – LCS   (local CS)  
       – TYPE   (history type code)  
       – NO0…NO9, C0…C9   (nine or ten numbered items, each with code “NOi” and value “Ci”)  
       – YMIN, YMAX   (global min/max for the entire history)  
       – TMIN, TMAX   (time or load step interval)  
       – TDIM   (time or step dimension)  
       – YTOL   (tolerance on Y values)  
       – LIM1, LIM2   (optional limit flags or values)  
       – TEFF, CLIM, XTYP, NX, TITL   (miscellaneous additional flags, climate codes, axis types, number of points, title)  

8.  ECHO, OPT, VAL  
    •  These three are listed together as a reminder that they are valid record names (defined elsewhere).  – ECHO toggles listing of input.  – OPT holds global options.  – VAL defines user parameters or variables.  

Additional records HEAD, END, and PAGE exist but are documented in the general SOFiSTiK Installation & Basics manual; they do not appear in this table.  

Usage Note for RAG: Index each record name as the document “title,” and store its item‐list as searchable keywords or attributes.  You’ll then be able to retrieve, for example, all records that include a “TMAX” field, or search for any record whose items include both “LCS” and “COMP.”

The input table is a concise specification of plotting parameters used in SOFiSTiK’s FEA/STRUCTURAL installation. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and covers seven configurable keywords. Below is a structured, detailed breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store.

1. General Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword or parameter name.  
     – Description: what the keyword controls and any permissible values.  
     – Unit: the measurement unit or data type (if applicable).  
     – Default: the built-in value used when no explicit setting is provided.  
   • Usage Context  
     – These keywords appear in plotting or result-representation commands.  
     – Related commands: SCHH (horizontal scale details), HIST (vertical range override).  
     – Additional reference: SOFiSTiK general manual, “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics.”

2. Items and Their Roles  
   1. DINA  
      • Controls the paper format size for output.  
      • Positive values select landscape orientation; negative values select portrait.  
      • Unit: none.  
      • Default: –4 (legacy reference to a predefined DINA format).

   2. S (Scale)  
      • Governs vertical scaling of plotted function values.  
      • Value “0” forces filling the available format fully.  
      • Asterisk “*” invokes an automatic “engineering scale” that best fits the page.  
      • Unit: none.  
      • Default: * (automatic engineering scale).

   3. W (Width)  
      • Specifies the paper width in centimeters.  
      • Overrides the DINA value if given.  
      • Unit: cm.  
      • Default: same as DINA setting.

   4. H (Height)  
      • Specifies the paper height in centimeters.  
      • Overrides the DINA value if given.  
      • Unit: cm.  
      • Default: same as DINA setting.

   5. MARG (Margin/Border Drawing)  
      • Dictates whether and how a frame border is drawn around the plot.  
      • Options (literal strings):  
         – OFF: no border lines.  
         – NO: draws only the inner border.  
         – YES: adds a free (user-defined) border around the content.  
         – FULL: draws both inner and outer borders up to the paper limits.  
      • Unit: LIT (literal).  
      • Default: FULL (complete border).

   6. FORM (Border Form)  
      • Chooses the style of the frame border.  
      • Options:  
         – STAN: standard SOFiSTiK frame.  
         – ZTVK: ZTVK-88 specification frame.  
      • Unit: LIT (literal).  
      • Default: STAN.

   7. TMAX (Time/Frequency Maximum)  
      • Sets the maximum time or frequency on the horizontal axis.  
      • Unit: sec/Hz.  
      • Default: * (automatic selection).  
      • Notes:  
         – The software auto-scales the horizontal axis in an “engineering manner” based on data magnitude.  
         – For large time spans, units switch to minutes or days automatically.  
         – Overriding TMAX can force a specific range for comparative plotting.

3. Cross-References and Overrides  
   • Horizontal Scale: governed by TMAX or auto-engineering logic; see SCHH for deeper control over tick spacing.  
   • Vertical Range: primary scale via S; full manual range override via HIST.  
   • Page Layout Flexibility: DINA ↔ W/H interplay allows both standardized and custom paper sizes.

This description captures the semantic structure, default behaviors, acceptable inputs, and interrelationships of the table entries, making it well suited for storage and retrieval in a vector-based RAG system.

The source table defines five configurable height parameters (H1–H5) that control the sizing of legend and axis annotations in a charting or technical‐drawing environment.  Each parameter is expressed in centimeters (cm) and carries a default value that remains active until redefined—either by a new invocation of the SIZE setting or via an SCHH command.  Setting any of these values to zero will suppress its associated annotation without affecting the others.

1. Item H1 – “Height of the legend”  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 2.50  
   • Purpose: Determines the overall vertical size (text plus surrounding space) reserved for the legend block.  A larger H1 yields a more prominent legend region; setting H1 = 0 completely suppresses the legend’s display.  

2. Item H2 – “Texts of the legend”  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 0.25  
   • Purpose: Specifies the nominal line height for each legend entry’s text.  This sub‐height is used to space individual labels within the legend.  If set to zero, legend labels are omitted (though the legend frame defined by H1 may still appear if H1 > 0).  

3. Item H3 – “Designation of the axes”  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 0.25  
   • Purpose: Controls the height—or baseline offset—for axis titles and designation text (e.g., “X-axis,” “Y-axis”).  Adjusting H3 lets you scale axis labels independently of general legend or tick‐mark text.  A zero value hides all axis title text.  

4. Item H4 – “Dimensional lines at the axes”  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 0.25  
   • Purpose: Governs the vertical clearance for dimension lines, arrowheads, and tick labels positioned along chart axes.  Tuning H4 changes the gap between the axis line itself and any attached measurement markers or numerical labels.  Setting H4 = 0 removes these dimension lines and their labels.  

5. Item H5 – “reserved”  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 0.18  
   • Purpose: Reserved for future expansion—no immediate effect under current versions.  It follows the same semantics as H1–H4 (zero suppresses) but is not yet tied to a visible chart element.  

Additional Context:  
• The SIZE parameter typically initializes these H-values en masse to scale a complete drawing.  
• SCHH provides a mechanism to override or redefine individual H-items on the fly.  
• Once set (either by SIZE or SCHH), each H value persists until explicitly changed again.  

By indexing H1 through H5 and pairing each with its description, unit, and default, this table supplies a clear, programmatic way to manage typographic and spacing rules for legends, axis labels, and dimension lines in a vector‐based plotting or CAD system.

See also: SIZE
 SCHH
 A value of 0. suppresses the corresponding designation. The values remain valid until a new definition of SIZE or SCHH is given.

The RESP table defines how the steady-state or transient response of a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillator is to be generated and plotted over a frequency (or period) sweep, for one or more damping values, and optionally compared against up to three external reference curves.  It is called after an excitation record (EXCI) and—if needed—after user-defined functions (FUNC) that supply reference data.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown:  

1. Item: TYPE  
   • Description: Selects which response quantity to compute and plot.  Literal values (LIT) are entered.  
     – P: Force (spring force or restoring force)  
     – S: Displacement (relative oscillator displacement)  
     – V: Velocity (relative)  
     – A: Relative acceleration (default)  
     – AA: Absolute acceleration (ground plus oscillator)  
     – AS: Acceleration as function of displacement (plots A vs. S)  
     – AAS: Absolute acceleration as function of displacement  
     – You may also suffix any of the above with “+” or “–” (e.g. P+, AA–) to plot only positive or negative signal components.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: A  

2. Item: TMIN  
   • Description: Lowest natural period (or highest frequency, if inverted) in the sweep.  
   • Unit: sec  
   • Default: 0  

3. Item: TMAX  
   • Description: Highest natural period (or lowest frequency) in the sweep.  
   • Unit: sec  
   • Default: “!” (symbolic; must be replaced by a concrete value)  

4. Item: TDIF  
   • Description: Increment step for the period (sec) or for the frequency (1/sec).  
     – If left “*”, the default step is (TMAX–TMIN)/20.  
   • Units: sec or 1/sec  
   • Default: *  

5. Items: D1, D2, D3, D4, D5  
   • Description: Up to five modal damping ratios (ζ) to evaluate in parallel.  
     – Each value is plotted with its own marker:  
       D1 = “.”  
       D2 = “+”  
       D3 = “*”  
       D4 = “o”  
       D5 = “x”  
   • Unit: ― (dimensionless)  
   • Defaults: D1 = 0.0; D2 through D5 = blank (i.e. not used unless specified)  

6. Items: C1, C2, C3, C4, C5  
   • Description: Colour and line-type codes to use when drawing the response curve for each damping value D1–D5.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Defaults: All = 1001 (a line-type index defined in EXCI minus 1001, or a colour code)  
   • Note: To define a mix of colours and line styles, one standard practice is to reserve code 1001–1010 for line-types and 2001–9001 for colours; then combine them with the EXCI base code (e.g. 2001 + 3002 – 1001 = 4002).  

7. Items: REF1, REF2, REF3  
   • Description: Index numbers referring to up to three external reference curves.  These must have been defined in preceding FUNC records.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: blank (none)  

8. Items: RF1, RF2, RF3  
   • Description: Colour and line-type codes for each reference curve REF1–REF3.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 2001  

Usage notes:  
- The RESP record must follow the excitation definition (EXCI) that supplies the forcing time-history or spectral input.  
- The solver will evaluate the SDOF equation only at the time points defined in the excitation function; ensure the excitation extends slightly beyond the highest frequency band edge (e.g. by appending zero-value tails) when high-frequency content is present.  
- By specifying multiple damping values D1–D5, you can generate comparative curves in a single run; the C-fields control how each appears graphically.  
- Reference curves (REF-fields) allow overlay of analytical or empirical data for benchmarking.

sections: 2.5 RESP – Properties of the Single Mass Oscillator

content:
See also: EXCI, SPEC
 RESP
 The single mass oscillator, which is subjected to the various excitations, must be described via a frequency range with fixed subdivisions.
 In the case of excitation through an acceleration, TYPE AA can be used to plot the total accel-
 eration (ground+oscillator). This is usually the desired value. For TYPE one can also enter P+, S+, V+, A+, AA+ as well as P-, S-, V-, A-, AA-. Then only the positive or negative components are evaluated.
 The evaluation of the oscillation equations is performed only for the times defined by the exci- tation function. The duration of the evaluation is also determined by the highest time value of the excitation value. A somewhat longer time range with exciting function 0.0 should thus be defined in the case of high frequency excitation.
 Up to five different damping values can be examined simultaneously. The damping values D1 through D5 can be used arbitrarily according to the desired marking. Different line types and colour values can be defined for the curves. The colour values and the line types are added here to the values defined inthe record EXCI minus 1001 (e.g. 2001 ”+” 3002 - 1001 = 4002). Therefore it is reasonable to input one record with line types (1001 through 1010) and the others with colours (e.g. 1001 through 9001).
 Up to three external reference curves may be shown. These functions have to be defined via FUNC and must be defined after an external load function for the response analysis.

The table shown below defines the five elemental “fields” that make up a single excitation- or comparison-function record in the DYNR input sequence.  Each record you enter into a FUNC section must supply values (or rely on defaults) for these fields in the order shown.  The table columns are:

  • Item  
    – The mnemonic code used in the data stream to identify which field is being set.  
  • Description  
    – A brief English phrase describing the role of that field.  
  • Unit  
    – The physical unit (if any) associated with the value.  A dash (—) indicates a dimensionless quantity.  LIT24 denotes a 24‐character literal string.  
  • Default  
    – The symbol or code that describes what happens if you do not explicitly supply a value:
      * “!” means the value must be provided by the first function point and thereafter is carried forward (there is no built-in default beyond “undefined”).
      * “*” means that a system default is used when you omit this field.
      * “–” means “no default”—you must explicitly set or supply this item (in practice, TITL also must appear at first use).

Table layout:

| Item | Description        | Unit   | Default |
|------|--------------------|--------|---------|
| T    | Time value         | sec    | !       |
| F    | Function value     | —      | !       |
| DT   | Time subdivision   | sec    | *       |
| NO   | Number of function | —      | *       |
| TITL | Title of function  | LIT24  | –       |

Detailed field notes:

1. T (Time value, sec, Default = ! )  
   – Represents the independent variable (time coordinate) of the oscillator excitation.  
   – Because the underlying mass is unity, “force” and “acceleration” differ only by a constant, so both use the same F field.  
   – The first data point of a new function must specify T explicitly; thereafter, if you omit T, the program assumes the last time plus the previous time increment (DT or the last ΔT).  Regularly spaced data need only supply the first T and DT.

2. F (Function value, dimensionless, Default = ! )  
   – The dependent variable (either an acceleration amplitude or a normalized force value) sampled at each time point.  
   – Like T, this field must appear for every data row defining the function curve.

3. DT (Time subdivision, sec, Default = * )  
   – A suggested or enforced time‐step subdivision for interpolating or plotting the function.  
   – If omitted, DYNR uses the last DT entered; if no DT has been entered since the current function began, a system default time increment is applied.

4. NO (Number of the function, dimensionless index, Default = * )  
   – An integer identifier that tags this set of T–F data to one of the multiple functions stored in the database.  
   – If you do not explicitly set NO, the database assigns the next available function index.  
   – Once you enter NO in the first data row of a function definition, it remains in effect until you begin a new function.

5. TITL (Title of the function, up to 24 characters, Default = – )  
   – A short text label to identify the function in list or report output (for example, “HIST-CURVE” or “LOADCASE-A”).  
   – Must be supplied the first time you define a new function; thereafter, the title persists.

Additional behavior (from the FUNC context block):

  • All excitation functions you define (their entire T–F histories) are stored in the RAG database and remain valid until you issue a new FUNC record or begin HIST or SPEC input.  
  • Entering any new FUNC data after HIST or SPEC will clear all previously stored functions.  
  • NO and TITL need only appear on the first data line of a new function group.  
  • By combining T/DT logic and the default-carrying mechanism, you can economize on input by supplying only the first time and using uniform spacing.  

See also the EXCI, SPEC, and HIST record types for related definitions of excitation curves, spectral functions, and historical response output.

See also: EXCI, SPEC, HIST
 FUNC
 Any functions that can be selected either as acceleration or loading of the single mass oscillator or as comparison curves to HIST can be defined in DYNR. Since the mass of the single mass oscillator is 1.0, no need of the differentiation exists there between acceleration and force.
 The values of all excitation functions get stored in the database. They are maintained until a new definition takes place. If FUNC values are input after the records HIST or SPEC, all functions are automatically deleted.
 NO and TITL are input by the first function value only. If no time value is entered, the last time increment is added to the last time value. In this case for regular time intervals the input of time values can be omitted for all higher values.

The following is a structured, detailed description of the input table for the EXCI command, suitable for ingestion into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) vector store. It explains the role of each parameter (“Item”), its meaning (“Description”), the expected data type or unit (“Unit”), and any default values or behaviors (“Default”). Where relevant, cross-references to RESP, FUNC, and the overall context in DYNR are noted.

1. Context and Purpose  
   • EXCI is the command that “activates” one or more excitation variation curves stored in the database.  
   • All curves selected via EXCI are plotted simultaneously.  
   • The selection remains in effect until another EXCI definition is given.  
   • If excitation variations were defined originally by FUNC in DYNR, they must be invoked by specifying LCS=0 (see FUNC).  
   • If EXCI is omitted entirely, the system defaults to the first function defined by FUNC.  

2. Table Overview  
   Columns:  
     – Item: Parameter name as used in the EXCI record.  
     – Description: Purpose and effect of that parameter.  
     – Unit: Expected data type or literal enumeration (LIT).  
     – Default: Value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

3. Detailed Parameter Breakdown  

   A. LCS (Storage Number of the Curve)  
     • Description: Index or slot in the internal curve database. Identifies which pre-defined excitation curve to activate.  
     • Unit: None (integer index).  
     • Default: “!” (mandatory) – must be provided unless invoking the special case of FUNC-origin curves (LCS=0).

   B. NO (Node Number of the Excited Point)  
     • Description: Finite-element node at which the excitation is applied. Determines the spatial location of the dynamic load or motion.  
     • Unit: None (integer node ID).  
     • Default: “!” (mandatory) – you must specify which node is being excited.

   C. COMP (Excitation Components)  
     • Description: Spatial directions in which loading or motion is imposed. Enumerated literal (LIT).  
     • Possible Values:  
         • X – X direction only  
         • Y – Y direction only  
         • Z – Z direction only  
         • XY – X and Y directions  
         • XZ – X and Z directions  
         • YZ – Y and Z directions  
         • XYZ – all three axes simultaneously  
     • Unit: LIT (literal flag).  
     • Default: XYZ – if omitted, excitation is applied in all directions by default.

   D. F (Colour and Line Type for the Curve)  
     • Description: Graphical attributes for plotting the selected curve: color index and line-style code. Reference SOFiSTiK general manual section “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics” for available codes.  
     • Unit: None (integer code).  
     • Default: 1001 – a standard plotting style if you don’t specify an alternative.

   E. TITL (Title of the Function)  
     • Description: User-defined text (up to 24 characters) to label the excitation curve in graphical outputs or listings. Helps identify multiple curves when plotted simultaneously.  
     • Unit: LIT24 (24-character literal).  
     • Default: “–” (blank) – no title shown unless provided.

4. Usage Notes and Cross-References  
   • To activate a variation curve defined via the FUNC record in DYNR, set LCS=0. The system then uses the first function defined by FUNC as the excitation.  
   • Once you input an EXCI record, its settings (LCS, NO, COMP, F, TITL) remain in force for subsequent analyses until a new EXCI appears.  
   • The EXCI command affects post-processing and plotting only; it does not alter the underlying structural model.  
   • For parameter RESP (response items to be extracted) and additional FUNC details, see the corresponding manual sections.

See also: RESP, FUNC

 If the excitation variation were defined in DYNR by the record FUNC, such a function must be selected with LCS 0. The first defined function FUNC is used, if EXCI is not input.

Below is a comprehensive description of the “TYPE” parameter as it appears in the SPEC/HIST table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store. This write-up covers the column definitions, permitted values, units, defaults, and how TYPE interrelates with other records (RESP, FUNC, HIST) and parameters (TMIN, TMAX, TDIF).

1. Table Schema  
   • Item  
     – Parameter name; here it is always “TYPE.”  
   • Description  
     – A concise natural-language explanation of what TYPE controls and its permitted literal values.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates the expected unit or data class for the parameter; specified as LIT (literal string).  
   • Default  
     – The fallback value used when no explicit TYPE is provided; here it is TIME.

2. Parameter: TYPE  
   – Purpose: Determines whether subsequent axis coordinates and grid divisions are interpreted in the time domain, the frequency domain, or on logarithmic scales.  
   – Location: Can appear in SPEC or HIST records. Upon processing a SPEC or HIST record, the system renders a new plot using all current settings, including TYPE.

3. Allowed Literal Values  
   • TIME  
     – Standard linear time axis. All derived parameters (TMIN, TMAX, TDIF) refer to time values.  
   – Interpretation: X-axis units are seconds (or the base time unit in context).  
   • FREQ  
     – Standard linear frequency axis. Causes RESP attributes TMIN, TMAX, TDIF to be treated as frequencies (e.g. Hz).  
   – Interpretation: Shifts the domain from time to frequency. Useful for spectrum or transfer-function plots.  
   • LOGT  
     – Logarithmic time axis. TMIN, TMAX denote time endpoints; TDIF is no longer a linear increment but a subdivision factor.  
   – Interpretation: A log-10 scale along the time axis. The number of intermediate grid lines is computed as 1.0/TDIF.  
   • LOGF  
     – Logarithmic frequency axis. Analogous to LOGT but applied to frequency.  
   – Interpretation: Plot frequency on a log-10 scale; subdivisions determined by TDIF.

4. Interaction with Other Parameters  
   • TMIN, TMAX, TDIF (from RESP record)  
     – Under TIME or LOGT: represent time start, end, and division.  
     – Under FREQ or LOGF: interpreted as frequency start, end, and division.  
     – TDIF semantics:  
       · Linear modes (TIME/FREQ): the step size between adjacent grid lines.  
       · Log modes (LOGT/LOGF): the reciprocal of TDIF gives the count of equal–log-step subdivisions. For example, TDIF=0.05 yields 20 subdivisions per decade.  
   • RESP record  
     – Defines the response data and its domain endpoints. When TYPE=FREQ or LOGF, RESP’s T-fields are treated as frequency parameters.  
   • FUNC record  
     – May supply mathematical functions or transfer expressions; evaluated over the axis defined by TYPE.  
   • HIST record  
     – Like SPEC, when HIST appears, it triggers a rendering. TYPE remains in force, controlling the domain for histogram or batch-plot output.

5. Default Behavior  
   – If TYPE is omitted, it defaults to TIME. The system produces a time-domain plot with linear spacing equal to the value of TDIF, spanning from TMIN to TMAX.

6. See Also  
   • RESP – for defining the numerical data or function arguments.  
   • FUNC – for specifying analytical expressions.  
   • HIST – for generating history-style or multi-trace plots.  
   • SPEC – for one-off or parameter-scan visualizations.

By indexing this description, a RAG system can quickly retrieve the role of TYPE, its valid settings, and how it influences other parameters—ensuring correct interpretation of time vs. frequency and linear vs. logarithmic axes whenever SPEC or HIST records are processed.

 If LOGT or LOGF are defined, a logarithmic scale is selected. TDIF defines then a subdivision factor relative to 1.0 for the number of intermediate values (e.g. TDIF 0.05 = 20 intermediate values).

The snippet you’ve provided documents the “HIST” plotting record in a classic FEM‐postprocessor and defines the parameters you must supply in order to generate one or more transient curves on a single graph.  Below is a structured, field-by-field breakdown of the little “table” plus its surrounding explanatory text.

1. Record name  
   • HIST  
   – Indicates you are defining a time‐history plot (transient curves).

2. Parameter 1: NX  
   • Meaning: index number for the data series within a given load case.  
   • Semantics: you may request up to ten separate curves (1 ≤ NX ≤ 10) in the same picture; each NX picks out one XTYP/LCS combination.  
   • Dependencies: NX ties directly to the XTYP code (what quantity to plot) and the load case number LCS.  

3. Parameter 2: TITL  
   • Meaning: an alphanumeric “title” or designation string for the graph.  
   • Usage: will appear as the chart title or legend heading.  

4. Parameter 3: DUMP  
   • Meaning: name of an external text file into which the time‐history data will be written.  
   • Notes: this parameter is optional (“Lt*” in the original table) — if specified, the processor creates a flat dump of the plotted data under that filename.  

5. Unit and Default Columns (implicit)  
   • Unit column: indicates what physical units the dumped data carry; usually inherited from the definition of XTYP (e.g. mm, rad, N, Pa, °C).  
   • Default: typically “*” (an asterisk) which means “use the built-in default” if you omit the field.

—  After the miniature table, the text goes on to explain how “HIST” behaves and how it interacts with the other plotting records (SIZE, FUNC, SPEC):

• Curve‐count and autoscaling  
  – You may plot up to ten curves (NX = 1…10) in one window.  
  – The Y‐ and T‐axes are autoscaled based on the data plus any overrides you give in a preceding SIZE record (via YMIN/YMAX or TMIN/TMAX).  
  – If you supply LIM1 and/or LIM2, then constant horizontal limit lines are drawn; they only appear if the data range exceeds YTOL × (limit value).

• Permissible XTYP codes (for both X- and Y-axes)  
  – Displacements: U-X, U-Y, U-Z  
  – Rotations: U-RX, U-RY, U-RZ  
  – Velocities: V-X, V-Y, V-Z, angular V-RX, V-RY, V-RZ  
  – Accelerations: A-X, A-Y, A-Z, angular A-RX, A-RY, A-RZ  
  – Spring forces/moments: P, PT, SPX, SPY, SPZ, SPXX, SPYY, SPZZ  
  – Truss/cable forces: TRUS, CABL  
  – Beam internal forces & moments: N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ  
  – Stresses: SIG, TAU, SIGV; in shells MXX, MYY, MXY; shell shears VXX, VYY; shell axials NXX, NYY, NXY  
  – Fluid/thermal: H, PN (pressure), QH, QBH, QHPI (flow rates), VQUA, VBRI (velocity), TKP, TDN (turbulence k/ε), T (temperature), QT, QBT, QTPI (heat flows), QQUA, QBRI (heat densities)  
  – Impedance coefficients: DSX, DSY, DSZ (1/displacements SX, SY, SZ), DSRX, DSRY, DSRZ (1/rotations SRX, SRY, SRZ)  
  (Any valid code may be mixed in one picture; the codes are repeatedly listed in the original manual.)

• Node-direction shifting  
  – If you want to plot different directional components for the same node in one graph, you append .0/.1/.2/.3 to the node number.  
    e.g. 1001.0 = U-X of node 1001, 1001.2 = U-Z.

• Comparison curves via FUNC  
  – You can define computed or comparative curves using a FUNC record.  
  – To include a function rather than a straight database curve, put the negative function number into one of your NX slots and set LCS = 0.  
  – If you only want function plots (no raw data), simply give LCS = 0 for all.

• LIM1/LIM2 enhancements  
  – You may also choose special limit lines: MEAN, SDEV, MAX, MIN, MAMI, or RMS.  
  – These draw horizontal reference lines at the statistical value you specify.

• Output  
  – Each HIST (and each SPEC) record drives one plotted output “picture.”  
  – The final graph shows your TITL, up to ten overlaid curves, autoscaled axes, any limit lines, and—if requested—a data dump in ASCII.

The table titled “ECHO” defines two configuration parameters used to control how output is echoed or rendered as text. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and contains two rows, one for each parameter. Below is a detailed description suitable for inclusion in a RAG vector store, capturing both structure and semantics:

1. Table Structure  
   - Columns:  
     • Item: The short name or code for the configuration parameter.  
     • Description: A brief explanation of what the parameter controls, sometimes expanded with a secondary clause.  
     • Unit: The data type or domain of permissible values. Here, both entries use the literal type (“LIT”).  
     • Default: The out-of-the-box setting applied when no user override is provided.

2. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
   A. OPT  
   • Item Code: “OPT”  
   • Description:  
     – “ECHO option” indicates that this parameter determines whether echo functionality is enabled.  
     – Sub-line “FULL output also as text” clarifies that when set to its “FULL” setting, all echoed content will also be rendered in text form.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal values accepted)  
   • Default: FULL  
     – By default, OPT is set to “FULL,” meaning complete echoing with textual representation unless explicitly changed.  

   B. VAL  
   • Item Code: “VAL”  
   • Description:  
     – “Value of the output option” specifies that this parameter selects the nature or verbosity level of the echoed output.  
     – Sub-line “FULL extensive output” highlights that the “FULL” setting yields the most comprehensive form of output.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal values accepted)  
   • Default: FULL  
     – The default value “FULL” ensures that, unless overridden, the system will produce extensive or maximal detail in its output.

3. Usage Context  
   • Both parameters work in tandem to govern how a system’s echoing mechanism behaves—“OPT” toggles the feature on or off (and in the “FULL” case, forces textual rendering), while “VAL” dictates how much detail is included in that rendering.  
   • Having identical default values (“FULL”) implies the system prioritizes full verbosity and text-based echo out of the box.  

4. Vector Store Implications  
   • Item and Description fields can be indexed as primary metadata for quick retrieval of parameter roles.  
   • Unit and Default columns serve as secondary attributes, aiding in validation checks and default-state reconstructions when answering queries or regenerating configuration contexts.

The image is a two-dimensional line chart titled “Figure 3.1: Trapezoidal load 1.” It presents the dynamic load factor (vertical axis) as a function of excitation period (horizontal axis) for a single trapezoidal load history under three different damping ratios. The chart was generated by the DYNR program as part of a parametric study of trapezoidal loading shapes (this one being the first trapezoidal definition).

Axes and Scales  
• The horizontal axis is labeled “Period [sec]” and spans from 0 to 6 seconds, with tick marks and gridlines at integer values (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).  
• The vertical axis is labeled “Force [kN]” and ranges from 0.0 up to 2.0 kN, with major ticks at 0.2 kN intervals; the zero line is clearly marked.  

Curves and Damping Cases  
Three distinct curves illustrate how the dynamic load factor varies with period for damping ratios ζ = 0.000, 0.200, and 1.000:

1. Damping = 0.000 (undamped)  
   – Rendered as a smooth, solid black line at the top.  
   – Begins at exactly 1.0 kN when the period is near zero.  
   – Rises rapidly to a peak just below 1.9 kN at around 1.6 to 1.8 s, reflecting the strongest resonance.  
   – Beyond the peak, it decays monotonically, dropping to roughly 0.4 kN by T = 6 s.

2. Damping = 0.200 (moderate damping)  
   – Plotted with a solid line overlaid by plus-sign markers (“+”).  
   – Also starts at 1.0 kN at T ≈ 0.  
   – Reaches a lower maximum of about 1.4 kN near T = 1.5 s, indicating reduced amplification.  
   – Then falls off more steeply than the undamped curve, leveling out around 0.3 kN at longer periods.

3. Damping = 1.000 (heavy damping)  
   – Shown as the lowest continuous curve, without special markers.  
   – Initial value is again 1.0 kN at near-zero period, but it does not exhibit a pronounced peak.  
   – Undergoes a gentle decline from approximately 1.0 kN at T = 0 to about 0.2 kN at T = 6 s, reflecting strong energy dissipation.

Annotations and Legends  
• Directly above the plot area, three labels “Damping 0.000,” “Damping 0.200,” and “Damping 1.000” denote each curve in left-to-right order.  
• The legend is implicit in the line styles and marker choices rather than enclosed in a box.  
• A small arrowhead at the right end of the period axis emphasizes the increasing period direction.

Contextual Note  
This plot corresponds to the first trapezoidal load case defined in the DYNR input (titled ‘TRAPEZOIDAL LOAD 1’). The trapezoid is characterized by a rapid rise, a hold phase, and a drop-off (as specified by the user’s FUNC parameters). The resulting response spectra illustrate how the maximum dynamic force—and hence the dynamic load factor—depends both on the excitation period and on the assumed structural damping.

The image is a two‐dimensional plot titled “Figure 3.2: Trapezoidal load 2,” showing the variation of peak force (in kilonewtons) as a function of system period (in seconds) for three different damping levels. It is intended to illustrate the dynamic load factors produced by a trapezoidal time‐history input under zero, moderate, and high damping, as computed by the DYNR program.

1. Axes and Scale  
   • Horizontal axis (abscissa) is labeled “Period [sec]” and runs from 0.0 s (origin) up to 6.0 s, with major tick marks and numeric labels at 1.0 s increments.  
   • Vertical axis (ordinate) is labeled “Force [kN]” and spans from 0.0 kN up to 2.0 kN, with major ticks at 0.2 kN or 0.4 kN intervals; the apex of the scale is just under 2.0 kN.  
   • Both axes meet at the lower left corner and terminate in arrowheads indicating their positive directions.

2. Curves and Legend  
   Three distinct curves, each corresponding to a different damping ratio (ζ), are superimposed:  
   – ζ = 0.000 (undamped) appears as a smooth solid line without point markers.  
   – ζ = 0.200 (20% damping) is plotted using a series of “+” (plus) symbols connected by a light line.  
   – ζ = 1.000 (100% damping) uses “×” (cross) or star‐like markers joined by a dashed or thin line.

   A simple inline legend beneath the main title area (or just above the plot) identifies each curve in the order “Damping 0.000 Damping 0.200 Damping 1.000.”

3. Curve Shapes and Key Features  
   • At very short periods (T → 0.0 s), all three curves begin at a force level of approximately 1.0 kN, reflecting the quasi‐static load factor of unity.  
   • As the period increases from 0 to roughly 1.0–1.5 s, the force peaks:  
     – The undamped case (ζ = 0) attains the highest peak, about 1.85 kN, near T ≈ 1.2 s.  
     – The 20% damped case peaks at approximately 1.45 kN around T ≈ 1.4 s.  
     – The heavily damped case (ζ = 1.0) shows only a slight amplification, peaking near 1.10 kN at T ≈ 1.6 s.  
   • Beyond the peak region, all three curves decay monotonically as period increases: by T ≈ 6 s the forces have dropped to roughly 0.35 kN (undamped), 0.30 kN (ζ = 0.2), and 0.25 kN (ζ = 1.0).

4. Visual Styling  
   • Light grid lines are faintly visible in the background, helping to read off values against the tick marks.  
   • Marker symbols on the damped curves are spaced uniformly along the lines, indicating discrete evaluation points in the DYNR output.  
   • The plot is rendered in black and white (or grayscale), with line style and marker shape serving to distinguish the three damping scenarios.

5. Interpretation in Context  
   This graph demonstrates how increasing damping progressively reduces both the magnitude of dynamic amplification and the sharpness of the resonant peak for a trapezoidal input load. Embedding it in a RAG vector store allows indexing by keywords such as “trapezoidal load,” “dynamic load factor,” “damping effects,” and “response spectra,” as well as numerical features like peak values and corresponding periods.

This figure is a two‐dimensional plot of dynamic load factors (response spectra) for a single triangular input pulse, computed by the DYNR program for three different damping ratios. It is labeled “Figure 3.3: Triangular load” beneath the diagram. The key features are:

Axes and Scale  
• Horizontal axis (abscissa): labeled “Period [sec]” with a right‐pointing arrow. Tick marks appear at integer periods from 0.0 up to 6.0 seconds.  
• Vertical axis (ordinate): labeled “Force [kN]” with an upward‐pointing arrow. The scale runs from 0.0 kN at the origin up to about 1.5 kN at the top of the plot.  

Curves and Damping Ratios  
• Three distinct response curves are shown, each corresponding to a different viscous damping ratio in the single‐degree‐of‐freedom system:  
  – Damping = 0.000 (undamped)  
  – Damping = 0.200 (20 percent critical)  
  – Damping = 1.000 (100 percent critical)  
• The undamped response is the uppermost solid line: it starts at force = 1.0 kN when Period ≈ 0, rises to a pronounced peak of about 1.5 kN near a period of roughly 0.8–0.9 seconds, then decays monotonically as period increases beyond 1 sec, tailing off toward ~0.3 kN at 6 sec.  
• The 20 percent‐damped response is plotted with “+” markers. It also commences at 1.0 kN at very short periods, peaks more modestly (around 1.2 kN) at a slightly longer period (≈ 1.0–1.2 sec), and decays more rapidly than the undamped curve, falling to about 0.2–0.3 kN by 6 sec.  
• The heavily damped (100 percent) response is shown with “×” markers. It essentially flattens out near the unity gain (1.0 kN) for small periods, exhibits only a very gentle maximum just above 1.0 kN around Period ≈ 0.7–0.8 sec, and then steadily declines to approximately 0.15 kN by Period = 6 sec.  

Behavioral Interpretation  
• At very short periods (high‐frequency excitations relative to the pulse duration), all three curves converge to the static input amplitude of 1.0 kN because the system cannot develop inertial amplification.  
• The undamped system shows the largest amplification peak because there is no energy dissipation; as damping increases, peak amplification diminishes and shifts slightly toward longer periods, and the post‐peak decay is steeper.  
• Beyond about 3–4 sec, all curves asymptotically decrease at roughly similar rates, reflecting that for periods long compared to the pulse width, the system response approaches quasi‐static behavior scaled by the inverse of period.  

Overall, this graph quantifies how a triangular load pulse of unit amplitude and 1.0 sec rise‐and‐fall time excites a range of single‐degree‐of‐freedom systems, illustrating the classic dynamic amplification dependence on both natural period and damping ratio.

This example makes use of the three-story frame from the manual for the program DYNA in order to calculate a story response spectrum for the highest story. Prerequisite for that is an excitation function, which can model the earthquake in a more realistic manner than a sinusoidal excitation. The sinusoidal excitation can be clearly marked as a spike in the story response spectrum making the analysis quite meaningless. For this reason, without going in depth, an excitation function with a frequency of roughly 10 Hertz, created by a statistical process, was selected.
 First an oscillation analysis of the entire structure with the program DYNA is necessary. This is done e.g. by the following input:
 PROG DYNA
 HEAD THREE-STORY FRAME BASE POINT EXCITATION ! MAXIMUM VALUES U3 = 10.2 CM ; V = 1360 KN ; M = 2040 KNM ! 0.5 CM ; V = 92 KN ; M = 138 KNM ! 0.2 CM ; V = 56 KN ; M = 84 KNM ! NATURAL FREQUENCIES 1.501 / 3.185 / 4.862 (HERTZ) EIGE 3 REST STEP 200 0.06 LC 51 FUNC 0.0000 0.0000; 0.1000 -0.5765; 0.2000 0.1357 FUNC 0.3000 -0.5040; 0.4000 0.5614; 0.5000 0.6055 . . . ACCE 0 0.0 3.0 HIST U-Y 4 LCST 51 HIST A-Y 3 4 1 LCST 51 HIST MYA 1 3 1 LCST 51 END
 The time variation of the displacements as well as the accelerations of the upper node (No. 4) is now available in the database. Then DYNR plots both these variations and calculates the story response spectrum with the following input:

 HEAD RESPONSE SPECTRUM OF ROOF STOREY HIST 51 U-Y 4 1001 HIST 51 A-Y 4 2001 HIST 51 MYA 1 1001 2 2001 3 3001 RESP A 0 1.5 0.02 0.001 0.02 EXCI 51 4 Y 1001 EXCI 51 3 Y 2001 SPEC END

 HIST 51 U-Y 4 1001
 HIST 51 A-Y 4 2001
 HIST 51 MYA 1 1001 2 2001 3 3001
